**Lijia Zhang** (Chinese:张丽佳; pinyin:_Zhāng Lìjiā_; born May 12, 1964, in Nanjing) is a Chinese-born writer, journalist, social commentator and public speaker. Her work focuses on contemporary China, particularly social change, gender and women’s lives, economic transformation, inequality, shifting social values and China’s evolving role in the global order. She writes regularly in English for international publications.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-1)
Born in Nanjing, Zhang spent ten years working in a state-owned factory producing intercontinental missiles before becoming a journalist and writer. She is the author of the memoir “Socialism Is Great!”: A Worker’s Memoir of the New China and the novel Lotus, and co-author of the oral history China Remembers. Her journalism and commentary have appeared in publications including the South China Morning Post, The Guardian, Newsweek and The New York Times.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-2)
Zhang describes herself as a “cultural bridge” between China and the wider world—a role she regards as her self-appointed mission.
Lijia Zhang on Sky TV's discussion program with Francis Fukuyama in 2022

## Early life and education
[edit]
Zhang was born into a working-class family in Nanjing and grew up in severe poverty. In 1980, when she was sixteen, her family took her out of school so that she could earn money. She began working at a military factory producing intercontinental missiles. During her decade there, she found solace in literature and taught herself English, initially as an escape from the routine of factory life.
During the 1989 protest movement, Zhang organised workers at her factory in support of the student-led demonstrations. She later wrote about her experience of the movement for The New York Times.
Zhang went to Britain in 1990, where she studied journalism. She later returned to China and began working with foreign correspondents before establishing herself as a journalist and writer. In 2003, she studied creative writing at Goldsmiths, University of London, receiving an MA.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-3)

## Journalism and Career
[edit]
After returning to China in the early 1990s, Zhang began her journalism career by assisting foreign correspondents as a researcher, interpreter and fixer. She subsequently wrote for international newspapers and magazines, with her work examining China’s social, cultural and economic transformation.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-4)
Her articles and commentary have appeared in publications including the South China Morning Post, The Guardian, The Financial Times, Newsweek, The New York Times, The Independent, The Japan Times and the Far Eastern Economic Review. Her work explores inequality, shifting social values and China’s evolving role in the global order.
Zhang is also a commentator on China for international broadcast media. She has appeared on the BBC, Channel 4, CNN, NPR, ABC Australia and Al Jazeera. (Impact Podcast) In 2008, she was the subject of the BBC television documentary [Peschardt’s People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peschardt's_People "Peschardt's People"). In 2026, she was interviewed at length for the Impact Podcast about China’s social transformation and its relationship with the wider world.
Zhang co-authored China Remembers (Oxford University Press, 1999), an oral history of the People’s Republic of China.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-5)
Her memoir, “Socialism Is Great!”: A Worker’s Memoir of the New China, recounts her decade working in a missile factory during China’s reform era and her transition from factory worker to writer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-6) The hardback edition was published in the United States by Atlas & Co. in 2008, followed by a paperback edition from Random House a year later.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-7) The memoir has also been published in Australia, India, the Netherlands, Italy, France, Brazil, Poland, South Korea and Germany. Historian Jonathan Spence called it “a truly original contribution to our understanding of modern China”.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-8)

## Journalism and Career
Her first novel, Lotus, was published by Macmillan in 2017. Set in Shenzhen, it follows a young migrant woman who becomes a sex worker. The novel was inspired by Zhang’s discovery of a family secret: her grandmother had been sold to a brothel as a young woman.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-9) The novel explores migration, sexuality, gender and the tension between traditional expectations and individual aspirations in contemporary China. It was named one of NPR’s notable books of 2017[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-10) and was later discussed by Zhang on the BBC World Service’s World Book Club.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-11)
Zhang also writes short fiction. Her story “Permission” appeared in Silkroad magazine’s Short Story Anthology in 2017, while “Bright and Fragrant” was included in The Best Asian Speculative Fiction 2018.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-13)
She is currently completing a historical novel based on the life of Qiu Jin, a revolutionary and pioneering Chinese feminist who defied the social conventions of her time by unbinding her feet, wearing men’s clothing and organising an armed uprising against Qing rule.
Zhang writes primarily in English despite being a native Chinese speaker. She has said that the decision followed an unsuccessful attempt in the early 1990s to publish a Chinese-language book about Western perceptions of Mao Zedong. According to Zhang, the manuscript was rejected by Chinese censors for being considered “too negative”, after which she decided to write in English.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-14)
She has described writing in English as a form of liberation, both politically and creatively, while also acknowledging the linguistic and cultural losses involved in writing in a second language.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-15)

Historian Jonathan Spence called it “a truly original contribution to our understanding of modern China”.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-8)
texts.3:
## Journalism and Career
Her first novel, Lotus, was published by Macmillan in 2017. Set in Shenzhen, it follows a young migrant woman who becomes a sex worker. The novel was inspired by Zhang’s discovery of a family secret: her grandmother had been sold to a brothel as a young woman.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-9) The novel explores migration, sexuality, gender and the tension between traditional expectations and individual aspirations in contemporary China. It was named one of NPR’s notable books of 2017[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-10) and was later discussed by Zhang on the BBC World Service’s World Book Club.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-11)
Zhang also writes short fiction. Her story “Permission” appeared in Silkroad magazine’s Short Story Anthology in 2017, while “Bright and Fragrant” was included in The Best Asian Speculative Fiction 2018.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-13)
She is currently completing a historical novel based on the life of Qiu Jin, a revolutionary and pioneering Chinese feminist who defied the social conventions of her time by unbinding her feet, wearing men’s clothing and organising an armed uprising against Qing rule.
Zhang writes primarily in English despite being a native Chinese speaker. She has said that the decision followed an unsuccessful attempt in the early 1990s to publish a Chinese-language book about Western perceptions of Mao Zedong. According to Zhang, the manuscript was rejected by Chinese censors for being considered “too negative”, after which she decided to write in English.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-14)
She has described writing in English as a form of liberation, both politically and creatively, while also acknowledging the linguistic and cultural losses involved in writing in a second language.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijia_Zhang#cite_note-15)

**Yangzhou Asiastar Bus Co., Ltd** is a bus manufacturer based in Yangzhou, Jiangsu, China. Founded in 1998, it is a subsidiary of **Jiangsu Yaxing**. The company's brands include Yaxing, Yangtse, Eurise and AsiaStar. Yaxing buses are largely sold domestically in China, but also have a presence in a number of international markets. It is listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange.
Yangzhou Yaxing Motor Coach Co., Ltd., aka Asiastar, traces its origins to May 1949, when the Shanghai Military Control Commission assumed control of the former sapper squadron of the Kuomintang, renaming it the **Automobile Maintenance Firm of Logistics Department of East China Air Force of the Chinese People's Liberation Army**.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) This was moved to Yangzhou in April 1958, where it was merged with the Yangzhou Automobile Maintenance Factory as the **Yangzhou Automobile Maintenance and Manufacture Factory**, which began producing automobiles (branded Yunhe) and tractors (branded Gongnong), alongside farm equipment.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) After gaining experience, the factory began producing the JS130/JS140 heavy-duty trucks and JS340 dump trucks in the late 1960s, then began producing the JT661A bus chassis in 1979.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1)

The factory was renamed to the **Jiangsu Yangzhou Automobile Maintenance and Manufacture Factory** (江苏省扬州汽车修造厂) in 1981, and the first JT663 coach was built and delivered to the Eighth Team of Jiangsu Passenger Transportation Co., Ltd. in February 1981.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) The JT663 was the first dedicated bus chassis built and the factory was renamed again to the **Jiangsu Yangzhou Coach Manufacture Factory** (江苏省扬州客车制造厂) in 1985.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) The company continued to develop buses, launching the JS6879 coach in 1989 in cooperation with the Xi'an Highway Institute, as the first domestic sleeper coach.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) The factory was renamed again to the **Jiangsu Yangzhou Coach Manufacture Main Factory** (江苏省扬州客车制造总厂) in 1990.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1)
The JS6971 luxury inter-city tourism coach was launched in 1993, which marked the first use of a domestically-produced rear axle.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) The **Jiangsu Asiastar Bus (Group) Co., Ltd.** (江苏亚星客车集团有限公司) was founded in August 1996, followed by the **Yangzhou Asiastar Motor Coach Co., Ltd.** (扬州亚星客车股份有限公司 in September 1998, with the approval of the provincial government; Yangzhou Asiastar was then listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in August 1999.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1)

Asiastar started several joint ventures with western companies, including Mercedes-Benz, to further develop domestic manufacturing and quality controls. In 2009, Weichai Group entered into a strategic framework cooperation agreement with Yangzhou Asiastar and the People's Republic of China and laid the cornerstone for a new Yangzhou factory in 2011.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) In 2012, Yangzhou Asiastar formed a holding company named **Fengtai Bus and Coach International** (FTBCI, 厦门丰泰汽车).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) The company's second factory is located in the Xiamen Free Trade Zone, which specializes in electric buses.

Yaxing Motor Coach is a bus manufacturing brand under Shandong Heavy Industry Group, with Yangzhou Yaxing Motor Coach Co., Ltd. as its operating entity (established on September 28, 1998, with a history tracing back to 1949). The company's principal business is the development, manufacture, and sale of buses and parts; its products cover city buses, tourist coaches, group buses, and special-purpose vehicles, and it also offers a variety of power solutions, such as fuel-powered and pure-electric options. As a long-established enterprise in China's bus industry, Yaxing Motor Coach was once ranked first in sales nationwide for seven consecutive years, and later voluntarily delisted from the A-share market in 2024 due to operational difficulties. Currently, the company relies on technical support from Weichai Group's industrial chain to continue its product R&D and actively expand overseas markets.

Parent company
Yangzhou Yaxing Motor Coach Co., Ltd.
History
The company's predecessor was the Automobile Repair Station of the East China Air Force Logistics Department, established in May 1949, originally stationed in Shanghai. In 1958, the repair station was moved to Yangzhou and merged with Yangzhou Automobile Repair Factory to form Yangzhou Automobile Repair and Spare Parts Factory. In 1979, Yangzhou Automobile Repair and Spare Parts Factory designed and manufactured the JT661A Bus and a bus chassis. In 1985, the factory was renamed Yangzhou Bus Manufacturing Factory, officially entering an era of bus-focused production.
6
In 1988, Yangzhou Bus Manufacturing Factory, in cooperation with Xi'an Highway Institute, developed China's first sleeper bus, the JS6970 (or JS6670). In August 1996, Yangzhou Bus Manufacturing Factory was reorganized into Jiangsu Yaxing Bus Group, becoming one of the ten key enterprises in Jiangsu Province. In 1997, Yaxing Motor Coach and Germany's Mercedes-Benz jointly established the Yaxing-Benz Bus Company. On August 31, 1999, the company was listed on the
Shanghai Stock Exchange
, becoming the first listed company in Yangzhou.
5

Around 2000, Yaxing Motor Coach had ranked first in national bus sales for seven consecutive years. In 2006, Mercedes-Benz decided to terminate the cooperation and sold its 50% stake in Yaxing-Benz Company at a price of 1 euro. In 2011, the controlling stake in Yaxing Motor Coach was transferred without compensation from Yangzhou State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission to Weichai (Yangzhou) Investment Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of Shandong Heavy Industry Group.
5
In 2016, Yaxing Motor Coach achieved a net profit of 62.3078 million yuan, reaching an all-time high. From 2020 to 2023, Yaxing Motor Coach incurred a cumulative loss of approximately 689 million yuan.
6
On October 17, 2024, due to consecutive losses and negative net assets, Yaxing Motor Coach voluntarily delisted from the
Shanghai Stock Exchange
.
6
Corporate Governance
The controlling shareholder of Yaxing Motor Coach is Weichai (Yangzhou) Investment Co., Ltd., and its actual controller is Shandong Heavy Industry Group. The company has one General Manager, several Deputy General Managers, and one Chief Financial Officer, all appointed by the board of directors. The company implements the General Manager Responsibility System and has established the General Manager Office Meeting System, including the General Manager Office Routine Meeting, the General Manager Special Office Meeting, and the General Manager Situation Briefing Meeting, to make decisions on major matters in the company’s day-to-day operation and management. The company has formulated internal management systems such as the General Manager Work Rules.
10
To resolve the horizontal competition issue with Zhongtong Bus, also under Shandong Heavy Industry Group, the company voluntarily delisted from the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024, a move regarded as one of the important measures to solve this issue. The company has deposit and loan business transactions with its related party Shandong Heavy Industry Group Finance Co., Ltd. As of the end of June 2024, the company’s deposit balance in the finance company was RMB 337,061,800, accounting for 0.87% of the total deposits absorbed by the finance company.
6
Main Business

Yaxing Motor Coach's main business is the development, manufacturing, sales, import and export, and maintenance services of buses, special vehicles, agricultural vehicles, and automotive parts. The company's core business focuses on the development, manufacturing, and sales of buses.
3
The company has two major production bases in Yangzhou and Xiamen. The Yangzhou base was expanded and put into production in August 2013, equipped with domestically advanced bus production lines and product R&D laboratories; the Xiamen base covers a total area of 100,000 square meters and mainly produces high-tech new-energy hybrid buses, pure electric buses, and low-emission luxury buses, with products mainly oriented to export.
16
The company's products cover various models of buses ranging from 5 to 18 meters, including long-distance buses, school buses, high-end tourist buses, city buses, group buses, luxury RVs, and special-purpose vehicles, all of which are environmentally friendly and energy-saving buses.
16
The company's products are not only well-sold in the vast majority of first- and second-tier cities in China, but have also entered developed country markets such as
Europe
, the United States, and
Australia
, while being exported to more than 20 countries and regions including North America, Australia, Eastern Europe,
Southeast Asia
, Russia, the Middle East, and Africa. The company has established more than 500 dealership and after-sales service outlets at home and abroad, providing users with networked integrated services.
3
In recent years, the company has shifted its development focus to overseas markets, and its export business has seen considerable growth.
3
Intellectual Property
As of July 2026, Yangzhou Yaxing Motor Coach Co., Ltd. had 159 patent information entries, 14 trademark information entries, 23 copyright information entries, and 51 administrative licenses. The company received National High-Tech Enterprise Recognition in 2023 and was selected as a Provincial Filing Unit for Enterprise Intellectual Property Management Standard Implementation for 2025.
1

In 2026, an invention patent that was granted to the company, “CAE Analysis Method and Device for Overall Strength of Leaf Spring Bus” (CN122433387A), pertains to the technical field of leaf spring bus simulation analysis. This method can efficiently complete the overall vehicle strength simulation and improve design efficiency. In the same year, a utility model patent, “Vehicle Electric Defrosting Control System and Electric Bus” (CN224361128U), was granted. It pertains to the technical field of electric buses and can achieve precise temperature control through a combination of gear positions of wind speed and heating power.
1
The company's patented technologies also cover multiple fields including electric vehicle towing mode control, IoV intrusion detection, full-message wireless collection, vehicle network security communication, vehicle scheduling, bus brake assist, full-load-bearing frame optimization, body painting, battery overvoltage warning, and other areas.
4
Social Responsibility
The company's business involves public transportation life and bus manufacturing. The company attaches importance to social responsibility and is committed to improving its ESG performance.
12
The company has established and holds multiple certifications including the Environmental Management System (ISO14001:2015), the Occupational Health and Safety Management System (ISO45001:2018), and the Quality Management System (IATF16949:2016). In environmental management, the company implements the Pollutant Discharge Permit System, and in 2021 all kinds of pollutants were discharged in compliance with standards. In safety management, no safety accidents occurred at the company's production site in 2021.
12
The company's pure electric bus products have been launched in Singapore, Japan, and Latin America. On August 21, 2024, the company organized an "Experience China" event, hosting international students from Belt and Road countries to visit the enterprise. The company's products have served international events such as the Beijing Asian Games and the Olympic Games.
26
Important Events

From July 21 to 22, 2026, Yaxing Motor Coach appeared at the Shandong Heavy Industry Global Partner Conference (Vietnam) and showcased new energy products. In April 2026, Yaxing Motor Coach held the Tour and Group Product Renewal Launch Conference in Yangzhou, releasing the Orui New Power Business Vehicle and the X12 PRO 1+1 Tourist Coach. In February 2026, at the 20th Annual Review Event Influencing the Bus Industry, Yaxing Motor Coach's X15 Series Bus was honored as the "Star of High-end Business and Official Vehicles," and its X12PRO Series Bus was named the "Star of Customized Tourist Coach."
2
In March 2024, because a marine accident rendered a batch of buses worth approximately US$6.94 million undeliverable to a Saudi Arabian customer, Yaxing Motor Coach ultimately reimbursed the customer US$7.63 million. In January 2024, Yaxing Motor Coach signed a major sales contract worth US$74.05 million with Dallah Company, a Saudi Arabian customer.
29
In March 2023, at the 17th Annual Review Event Influencing the Bus Industry, Yaxing Motor Coach's JS6111XCE School Bus was named the "Star of Worry-free School Bus," and its JS6108GHFCEV Fuel Cell Bus received the "Fuel Cell Technology Innovation Achievement Award."
32
In December 2021, Yaxing Motor Coach held the Shandong Heavy Industry Weichai Power 2022 Business Conference Yaxing Branch and released the "Multi-dimensional Mobility" solution and multiple new products.
31
Emmerson Mnangagwa, President of Zimbabwe, once took a test ride in the YBL6148H, a Yaxing Motor Coach customized coach.
27
Corporate Culture

Yaxing Motor Coach's business philosophy emphasizes technological inheritance and serving the public, and regards "Customer Satisfaction is Our Tenet" as one of its core values. The company was founded in 1949 and is one of the brands with a relatively long history in the domestic bus industry. It places importance on its talent strategy and, in the course of development, focuses on environmental protection, energy conservation, and emission reduction.
3
The company's product philosophy emphasizes technological innovation and travel safety, and it adheres to the high standard of "Do not take the market as a testing ground, but take the testing ground as the market." In terms of safety, Yaxing Motor Coach adopts measures from the two dimensions of passive protection and active protection to ensure the safety of drivers and passengers.

**Yangzhou Asiastar Bus Co., Ltd** is a bus manufacturer based in Yangzhou, Jiangsu, China. Founded in 1998, it is a subsidiary of **Jiangsu Yaxing**. The company's brands include Yaxing, Yangtse, Eurise and AsiaStar. Yaxing buses are largely sold domestically in China, but also have a presence in a number of international markets. It is listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange.
Yangzhou Yaxing Motor Coach Co., Ltd., aka Asiastar, traces its origins to May 1949, when the Shanghai Military Control Commission assumed control of the former sapper squadron of the Kuomintang, renaming it the **Automobile Maintenance Firm of Logistics Department of East China Air Force of the Chinese People's Liberation Army**.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) This was moved to Yangzhou in April 1958, where it was merged with the Yangzhou Automobile Maintenance Factory as the **Yangzhou Automobile Maintenance and Manufacture Factory**, which began producing automobiles (branded Yunhe) and tractors (branded Gongnong), alongside farm equipment.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1) After gaining experience, the factory began producing the JS130/JS140 heavy-duty trucks and JS340 dump trucks in the late 1960s, then began producing the JT661A bus chassis in 1979.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yaxing_Coach#cite_note-History-1)

Yaxing Motor Coach is a bus manufacturing brand under Shandong Heavy Industry Group, with Yangzhou Yaxing Motor Coach Co., Ltd. as its operating entity (established on September 28, 1998, with a history tracing back to 1949). The company's principal business is the development, manufacture, and sale of buses and parts; its products cover city buses, tourist coaches, group buses, and special-purpose vehicles, and it also offers a variety of power solutions, such as fuel-powered and pure-electric options. As a long-established enterprise in China's bus industry, Yaxing Motor Coach was once ranked first in sales nationwide for seven consecutive years, and later voluntarily delisted from the A-share market in 2024 due to operational difficulties. Currently, the company relies on technical support from Weichai Group's industrial chain to continue its product R&D and actively expand overseas markets.

On April 1, 1927, the Kuomintang Jiangsu Provincial Headquarters moved to Nanjing. On April 9, right-wing KMT factions attacked left-wing provincial and municipal party headquarters and the General Labor Union,[115] arresting and executing several cadres in violence that continued through April 11.[116] On April 18, a faction aligned with Chiang Kai-shek established the National Government in the city,[117] which eventually asserted dominance over competing factions in Wuhan and Shanghai. On June 1, Nanjing was designated a Special Municipality and formally declared the national capital.
Nanking, 1927. Map compiled by the British War Office/U.S. Army Map Service.
The new regime launched the Capital Plan (首都計劃), an ambitious urban modernization scheme developed with the assistance of American architect Henry Murphy.[118] A central feature was the 12-kilometre Zhongshan Road axis, a 40-metre-wide thoroughfare connecting the riverfront at Xiaguan Pier to the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum.[119] The project required large-scale land requisitions and demolitions; prolonged delays in compensation provoked protests from local merchants and residents.[118]
Urban expansion was accompanied by administrative friction. Throughout the late 1920s and early 1930s, the Nanjing municipal government struggled with Jiangsu provincial authorities and Jiangning County over tax revenues and jurisdictional boundaries. The city's territory was officially enlarged from 157 to about 466 square kilometres in 1935. During the "Nanjing Decade", the city became a centre of research and education, home to National Central University, Academia Sinica, and the Purple Mountain Observatory. Political control, however, remained tight: the Xiaozhuang School (曉莊學校), founded by Tao Xingzhi to promote rural education, was forcibly closed in 1930 by government order, largely due to official concerns over its socially radical potential.[120]

Social stratification remained acute, with a 1934 survey finding that approximately 45.1 per cent of households lived in shantytowns concentrated primarily in the southern and western districts and the northern outskirts of Xiaguan,[121] while nearly 28 per cent of residents were officially registered without occupations, a diverse group ranging from the destitute and institutionalized to the very wealthy.[122] At the same time, Nanjing functioned as the hub of the Nationalist security apparatus, including organizations such as the Blue Shirts Society and the Central Bureau of Investigation and Statistics.
The basketball court of Nanjing Central Stadium, c. 1930
Although urban industrialization remained limited, the "Greater Nanjing" plan designated the riverfront as a heavy industrial zone. Notably, Yongli Chemical Industry Company's ammonia factory (永利錏厰) was established with government support in Luhe. Beginning operations in early 1937, the plant produced daily averages of 150 tons of ammonium sulfate and 40 tons of nitric acid by that summer. During the subsequent conflict, its chemical production capacity led to it being targeted by Japanese aerial bombardment.[123]
Japanese naval aircraft began heavily bombing Nanjing on August 15.[124] On August 21, the diplomatic representatives of the United States, Great Britain, France, Germany, and Italy in Nanjing jointly requested that the Japanese government instruct its bombers to avoid a specified area containing foreign embassies and shipping anchorages.[125] The Japanese Foreign Ministry declined, stating that the area contained Chinese military establishments. The Japanese Third Fleet commander warned on September 19 that air operations would commence on September 21 and demanded the evacuation of foreign nationals and warships. The United States Asiatic Fleet refused to withdraw, notifying the Japanese command that its gunboats would remain at Nanjing to protect the embassy and remaining civilians.[126] On September 22, the U.S. government formally protested the plan, stating it would jeopardize American lives and was contrary to the principles of law and humanity.[126]
As Japanese forces advanced rapidly into the Yangtze delta after the fall of Shanghai, the Chinese National Government began relocating its ministries and offices to the southwestern city of Chongqing in November to sustain long-term resistance.

After Japanese forces breached the designated lines of defense and converged on the capital from three directions, the Imperial General Headquarters in Tokyo issued the order for a concentrated assault on Nanjing on December 1. Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek and the Military Affairs Commission evacuated to Wuhan on December 7. Nanking: A Historical Background
The City

Nanking, China, is a city with a rich history that has played a central role in much of China’s history. It is the capital of the Jiangsu Province in Eastern China, and a port on the Yangtze River. The city, also spelled Nanjing or Nan-ching, was founded in the 8 th century BC. The city served as the national capital of China from the 3 rd to the 6 th century AD under many different names, in addition to parts of the 10 th, 14 th, and 15 th centuries. In 1421, Beijing became the imperial capital of China, whereupon Nanking was given its name, which it used until the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) when it was named Chiang-ning. Chiang-ning was opened to foreign trade in 1860 it remained an important treaty port for Chinese trade. In 1912, the city was renamed Nanking and made the provisional capital of the new Republic of China. 1927 saw Nanking taken by Communist control, but the city was retaken by Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek in 1928, when it was named the nation’s capital. In 1945, after the end of World War II, Nanking served as the capital of the republic of China until 1949, when Beijing was named the new capital of the People’s Republic of China. Nanking was developed as a heavy industry center, and in 1952, it was named a provincial capital. The city sports a rich cultural heritage, serving as a manufacturing center for cement, fertilizer, chemicals, electronic equipment, iron, steel, motor vehicles, and machine tools. The city has its own university, a theological seminary, and astronomical observatory. Nanking also hosts a bridge spanning the Yangzte River (built 1968), the tomb of Sun Yat-sen (built 1925-29), and the remnants of a 14 th century Ming emperor tomb. The 1990 population of Nanking was estimated at 2,090, 204.[[1]](https://web.stanford.edu/~kcook/history.html#_ftn1) Nanking has also been the host of events that occurred during World War II that were later to be labeled as the rape of Nanking.

In 1937, Nanking was seized by Japanese forces and held until 1945. Over the course of this capture, events indicate that Japanese soldiers enacted numerous counts of atrocities. The goal of this web site is to recount the events leading up to the rape of Nanking and to followup these events in as objective a manner as possible. The primary focus of this site is neither to condemn nor defend the events that occurred at Nanking. Rather, the aim of this site is to analyze these events from a sociological perspective and examine how these events could have occurred using the theories driving conformity and groupthink. This page gives a historical account of the events at Nanking that have been labeled as the rape of Nanking.
The First Sino-Japanese War and After
Tensions between China and Japan began escalating in the early 20 th century, precipitating the events at Nanking during World War II. The first Sino-Japanese War saw its roots in a conflict over Korea, which began as a tributary state of China. During the 19 th century, Japan grew as a military power and began looking towards taking control of Korea from the Chinese. Japan signed the Treaty of Kanghwa with Korea in 1876 in which a provision declared Korea unilaterally independent, weakening China’s hold on Korea. March of 1894, a domestic rebellion by the anti-foreigner Tonghak cult against the Korean monarchy was jointly put down by both Japanese and Chinese troops. After the revolt was quelled, China proposed the immediate withdrawal of foreign troops, which Japan ignored. During July of 1894, Japanese troops surprise attacked the Chinese troops in Korea, escalating events in Korea into the first Sino-Japanese War. The Japanese quickly defeated Chinese forces in Pyongyang and at sea and under the Terms of the Treaty of Shimonoseki, drafted on April 17, 1895, China was made to acknowledge complete independence of Korea, cede Taiwan, the P’enghu Islands, and Liaodong Peninsula in northern China to Japan and pay a war indemnity of 200 million taels. This first Sino-Japanese War set the stage for the second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945) of which the events at Nanking were a part.

During the interim between the first and second Sino-Japanese Wars, both China and Japan saw many militaristic changes. In China, two hundred years of Manchu ruler ship was put to an end with the rise of Nationalist rebels led by Dr. Sun Yat-sen. This movement drove to establish a republican government, and rebellions sprang up all over China during the middle of 1911. General Yuan Shih-k’ai, in charge of the Manchu armies, turned power over to the rebels in exchange for a position as president of the newly proposed republican government and on February 14, 1912, two days after Sun Yat-sen had stepped down as provisional president of China, a revolutionary assembly in Nanking elected Yuan Shih-k’ai the first president of the Republic of China, nailing down the lid of the coffin of the last of the dynastic rules in China and paving the way for a new and militant style of leadership in China. The Kuomintang party, under Dr. Sun Yat-sen’s leadership focused on reuniting China.

The Japanese, for their part, stepped away from their feudal roots of government and also took on a more militant style of leadership during the early part of the 20 th century. With the ancient philosophies of bushido, The Way of the Warrior, still deeply ingrained in the citizenry of Japan, The Japanese sought to advance their militaristic power. The Bushido philosophy placed the greatest honor a warrior could gain with serving his lord and ultimately the emperor with devoted loyalty. Under this philosophical framework, Japan began its military growth. Education in Japan became a means of programming a new nation of warriors. Students were groomed to desire to serve their nation, and the militaristic flavor of nation pervaded into the classrooms, where conformity and obedience to teacher demands to value obedience and unconditional loyalty to the emperor was the rule of the day. Physical training began in school with students being taught to march and wave flags in a disciplined and orderly fashion. The next logical step for most students was to serve in the military after school, where the pressure to conform to authority only increased. Obedience became the doctrine of the soldier and individual aims were made subservient to the desire to advance the goals of the nation. The Japanese military was rigorous, requiring 3,382 hours of class work and 2,765 hours of private study to earn an officer’s commission, some four thousand total hours more than what was required of an officer’s commission in England. Military forces continued to dominate Japanese government throughout the early 20 th century. One of the goals laid down by Japan during this time was to become a dominant power in Asia, a credo demonstrated by the first Sino-Japanese War and later during World War I. The Japanese saw expansion into China as a key play to gain military dominance, and World War I offered them the chance to push into China when, in 1915, Japan proposed the Twenty-one Demands that pushed China to become virtually a protectorate of Japan in addition to ceding more holdings to the Japanese. China signed a modified version of the Demands which placed more power over China in Japanese hands.

Nanjing also served as the capital of four other regimes over more than 1,000 years since the Six Dynasties period: the Southern Tang dynasty in the Five Dynasties period and Ten Kingdoms, the Ming dynasty, the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom and the Republic of China. After the Sui dynasty annihilated the Southern Chen dynasty and unified China, policies were adopted to suppress the status of Nanjing, given its reputation as the former capital of the Six Dynasties. While the city of Jiankang was destroyed, a new regional capital was instituted in Shitoucheng and was called Jiang Zhou (zhou means “province”), which was renamed Danyang Jun (Jun means “prefecture”) during the reign of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty. In the third year of Wude of the Tang dynasty (620), Danyang Jun was abolished and Yang Zhou was established. In the eighth year of Wude (625), the capital of Yang Zhou was relocated to Jiangdu (present-day Yangzhou, in Jiangsu Province). Since then, Yangzhou has been the proper name of the area in which Jiangdu was situated. In the second year of Zhide (757), Jiangning Jun was established in Jiangning Xian (xian means “county”) of Run Zhou, which was renamed Sheng Zhou in the following year. Thus, during the more than 300 years from the Sui dynasty to the Tang dynasty the administrative levels of the Nanjing area were no higher than zhou or jun and were in most cases xian. In the second year of the Wuyi (920) of the period comprising the Five Dynasties and the Ten Kingdoms, the regime of Yang Wu promoted Sheng Zhou to Jinling Fu (fu also means “prefecture”), declaring the first establishment of such a district in the Nanjing area. During the first month of the third year of Tianzuo (937), Jinling Fu was renamed Jiangning Fu. In the 10th month of that year, Xu Zhigao (also known as Li Bian), a powerful minister in the regime of Yang Wu, usurped the throne. With Jiangning Fu as the new capital, the dynasty he established became what is now referred to as the Southern Tang. In the Northern Song dynasty, Sheng Zhou was established in the Nanjing area, which was reestablished as Jiangning Fu.

It had been renamed Jiankang Fu during the Southern Song dynasty and was instituted as the secondary capital under the capital of Lin’an (present day Hangzhou, in Zhejiang Province) by Emperor Gao of the Southern Song in the eighth year of Shaoxing (1138). In the second year of Tianli of the Yuan dynasty (1329), Jiankang Lu (lu also means “prefecture”) was renamed Jiqing Lu. During the 16th year of Zhizheng in the Yuan dynasty (1356), Jiqing Lu was conquered by Zhu Yuanzhang and was renamed Yingtian Fu. In the 28th year of Zhizheng of the Yuan dynasty (1368, the second year of the Western Wu regime), Zhu Yuanzhang was crowned as Emperor of the Great Ming dynasty in Yingtian Fu. Because the Ming dynasty had adopted the system of a southern capital and a northern capital, Yingtian Fu was instituted as Nanjing (“southern capital”), representing the first time that the name Nanjing was used in reference to the area. This was also the point at which Nanjing became the capital of a unified China. During the 19th year of Yongle (1421), Zhu Di, also known as Emperor Cheng of the Ming dynasty, relocated the principal capital to Beijing, leaving Nanjing as the secondary capital. In the Qing dynasty, Yingtian Fu was reestablished as Jiangning Fu. During the third year of Xianfeng of the Qing dynasty (1853, the third year of Guihao of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom), Jiangning Fu was conquered by the Taiping army and made the capital of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, whereupon it was given the name Tianjing. Nanking: A Historical Background
The City
texts.1: Nanking, China, is a city with a rich history that has played a central role in much of China’s history. It is the capital of the Jiangsu Province in Eastern China, and a port on the Yangtze River. The city, also spelled Nanjing or Nan-ching, was founded in the 8 th century BC. The city served as the national capital of China from the 3 rd to the 6 th century AD under many different names, in addition to parts of the 10 th, 14 th, and 15 th centuries. In 1421, Beijing became the imperial capital of China, whereupon Nanking was given its name, which it used until the Qing dynasty (1644-1911) when it was named Chiang-ning. Chiang-ning was opened to foreign trade in 1860 it remained an important treaty port for Chinese trade. In 1912, the city was renamed Nanking and made the provisional capital of the new Republic of China. 1927 saw Nanking taken by Communist control, but the city was retaken by Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek in 1928, when it was named the nation’s capital. In 1945, after the end of World War II, Nanking served as the capital of the republic of China until 1949, when Beijing was named the new capital of the People’s Republic of China. Nanking was developed as a heavy industry center, and in 1952, it was named a provincial capital. The city sports a rich cultural heritage, serving as a manufacturing center for cement, fertilizer, chemicals, electronic equipment, iron, steel, motor vehicles, and machine tools. The city has its own university, a theological seminary, and astronomical observatory. Nanking also hosts a bridge spanning the Yangzte River (built 1968), the tomb of Sun Yat-sen (built 1925-29), and the remnants of a 14 th century Ming emperor tomb. The 1990 population of Nanking was estimated at 2,090, 204.[[1]](https://web.stanford.edu/~kcook/history.html#_ftn1) Nanking has also been the host of events that occurred during World War II that were later to be labeled as the rape of Nanking.
texts.2:
In 1937, Nanking was seized by Japanese forces and held until 1945. Over the course of this capture, events indicate that Japanese soldiers enacted numerous counts of atrocities. The goal of this web site is to recount the events leading up to the rape of Nanking and to followup these events in as objective a manner as possible. The primary focus of this site is neither to condemn nor defend the events that occurred at Nanking. Rather, the aim of this site is to analyze these events from a sociological perspective and examine how these events could have occurred using the theories driving conformity and groupthink. This page gives a historical account of the events at Nanking that have been labeled as the rape of Nanking.
The First Sino-Japanese War and After
Tensions between China and Japan began escalating in the early 20 th century, precipitating the events at Nanking during World War II. The first Sino-Japanese War saw its roots in a conflict over Korea, which began as a tributary state of China. During the 19 th century, Japan grew as a military power and began looking towards taking control of Korea from the Chinese. Japan signed the Treaty of Kanghwa with Korea in 1876 in which a provision declared Korea unilaterally independent, weakening China’s hold on Korea. March of 1894, a domestic rebellion by the anti-foreigner Tonghak cult against the Korean monarchy was jointly put down by both Japanese and Chinese troops. After the revolt was quelled, China proposed the immediate withdrawal of foreign troops, which Japan ignored. During July of 1894, Japanese troops surprise attacked the Chinese troops in Korea, escalating events in Korea into the first Sino-Japanese War. The Japanese quickly defeated Chinese forces in Pyongyang and at sea and under the Terms of the Treaty of Shimonoseki, drafted on April 17, 1895, China was made to acknowledge complete independence of Korea, cede Taiwan, the P’enghu Islands, and Liaodong Peninsula in northern China to Japan and pay a war indemnity of 200 million taels. This first Sino-Japanese War set the stage for the second Sino-Japanese War (1937-1945) of which the events at Nanking were a part.
texts.3: During the interim between the first and second Sino-Japanese Wars, both China and Japan saw many militaristic changes. In China, two hundred years of Manchu ruler ship was put to an end with the rise of Nationalist rebels led by Dr. Sun Yat-sen. This movement drove to establish a republican government, and rebellions sprang up all over China during the middle of 1911. General Yuan Shih-k’ai, in charge of the Manchu armies, turned power over to the rebels in exchange for a position as president of the newly proposed republican government and on February 14, 1912, two days after Sun Yat-sen had stepped down as provisional president of China, a revolutionary assembly in Nanking elected Yuan Shih-k’ai the first president of the Republic of China, nailing down the lid of the coffin of the last of the dynastic rules in China and paving the way for a new and militant style of leadership in China. The Kuomintang party, under Dr. Sun Yat-sen’s leadership focused on reuniting China.
texts.4: The Japanese, for their part, stepped away from their feudal roots of government and also took on a more militant style of leadership during the early part of the 20 th century. With the ancient philosophies of bushido, The Way of the Warrior, still deeply ingrained in the citizenry of Japan, The Japanese sought to advance their militaristic power. The Bushido philosophy placed the greatest honor a warrior could gain with serving his lord and ultimately the emperor with devoted loyalty. Under this philosophical framework, Japan began its military growth. Education in Japan became a means of programming a new nation of warriors. Students were groomed to desire to serve their nation, and the militaristic flavor of nation pervaded into the classrooms, where conformity and obedience to teacher demands to value obedience and unconditional loyalty to the emperor was the rule of the day. Physical training began in school with students being taught to march and wave flags in a disciplined and orderly fashion. The next logical step for most students was to serve in the military after school, where the pressure to conform to authority only increased. Obedience became the doctrine of the soldier and individual aims were made subservient to the desire to advance the goals of the nation. The Japanese military was rigorous, requiring 3,382 hours of class work and 2,765 hours of private study to earn an officer’s commission, some four thousand total hours more than what was required of an officer’s commission in England. Military forces continued to dominate Japanese government throughout the early 20 th century.
